title: Marguerite and the Bell
premise: Folklorist Rosalind Blackwood arrives in the drowned-valley village of Marguerite's Hollow to record its songs, but every singer stops at the same verse and the church bell that no one rings tolls once each night. Her sleep recordings reveal a second voice answering her questions in her own timbre: the Bell keeps a count of the village's debts, and the Blackwood name is on the ledger. To save her family she must learn what her grandmother paid to survive the last count, and in the end Rosalind takes the debt into herself, ringing the bell thirteen times so the village wakes with no memory and she remains as the new keeper of the count.
about_author: Ines Amberdale is a former archivist of oral histories who spent a decade collecting folk songs in remote valleys before turning to fiction. She writes horror rooted in the belief that every tradition is a contract someone signed on our behalf.

chapters.title: The Verse No One Finishes
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She arrives in Marguerite's Hollow, charmed by its crooked lanes, and records old Tam Yew singing a harvest song he abruptly refuses to finish, hands shaking. The emotional beat is professional curiosity curdling into unease when three other singers stop at the identical word.

chapters.title: One Toll at Midnight
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Woken by a single bell strike from the locked, roofless church, she finds villagers awake but pretending to sleep. Beat: first crack in her skepticism; the village's collective silence feels less like superstition than discipline.

chapters.title: Fieldwork
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She interviews the innkeeper's daughter, who recites genealogies like warnings, noting which families are 'counted' and which were 'struck off.' Beat: dread as Rosalind realizes the Blackwoods appear on no list at all — omitted, not absent.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Reviewing overnight recordings, she hears herself asking questions in her sleep — and something answering in a voice almost hers. It knows her grandmother's maiden name. Beat: terror; the evidence she came for is evidence against her.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Buried
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, with letters. In her late grandmother's trunk she finds a hymnal with pages cut out and a note: 'Never answer it after dark.' Beat: inheritance reframed as liability; family love shadowed by concealment.

chapters.title: Tam Yew's Confession
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, Tam then Rosalind. Dying Tam admits the village stopped singing the final verse because the last person who finished it was 'collected' in 1953 — the year a Blackwood survived. Beat: guilt passed down generations; Rosalind's unbelief begins costing others their comfort.

chapters.title: The Count Begins
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The bell tolls twice. Livestock dies in a perfect circle around the church, and every clock in the inn stops at 12:02. Beat: escalation; abstract folklore acquires a body count.

chapters.title: Questions in the Dark
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She deliberately sleeps wired to the recorder and asks the second voice directly what it wants. It answers: 'The balance. A Blackwood left owing.' Beat: grim clarity; negotiation replaces denial.

chapters.title: Sister of the Ledger
chapters.summary: POV of Maren, the innkeeper's daughter. Maren reveals the village keeps its own tally book and has been quietly deciding whether to give Rosalind up. Beat: betrayal; hospitality revealed as bookkeeping.

chapters.title: Thirteen Verses
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. In the church crypt she finds the song complete, carved into stone: thirteen verses, the thirteenth a payment schedule. Beat: awful comprehension; the song was never art, it was an invoice.

chapters.title: The Flight That Fails
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She packs her family's things and drives out; the road loops back to the Hollow no matter the direction, and the bell tolls three times at dawn. Beat: despair; escape is a verse the Bell has already heard.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV via recovered tape, 1953. A recording surfaces of young Edith Blackwood bargaining with the voice: her life for a deferral, 'until another Blackwood asks.' Beat: heartbreak; survival was purchased, and Rosalind is the interest coming due.

chapters.title: Village of Creditors
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. The village splits — some want to help Rosalind pay, some want her taken whole. Tam dies mid-sentence, his last word the forbidden verse's final syllable. Beat: moral fracture; fear makes neighbors into accountants.

chapters.title: What the Voice Is
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Researching the valley's flooding, she learns the original Marguerite rang the bell to warn of the dam break and was blamed for the panic that killed thirty-one. Beat: tragic reframe; the monster began as a warning no one thanked.

chapters.title: An Answer Given Freely
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Following the note's rule inverted, she answers the voice after dark — willingly, aloud, offering herself. The bell tolls seven times; the counting accelerates. Beat: courage entangled with hubris; she thinks she's found a loophole.

chapters.title: The Hollowing
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Villagers begin forgetting Rosalind — photographs blank, letters unreadable — as the Bell 'collects' her by erasure rather than death. Beat: horror of being unwritten; memory itself becomes the currency.

chapters.title: Maren's Choice
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren defies the tally book, hiding Rosalind in the crypt and reading the thirteenth verse aloud to find the exit clause. Beat: loyalty against communal pressure; friendship as defiance.

chapters.title: The Exit Clause
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The clause requires a keeper: someone must ring the bell thirteen times and hold the count forever, remembered by no one. Beat: the price made explicit; survival means being forgotten by everyone you save.

chapters.title: Last Night in the World
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She spends one real evening with her family, recording them laughing, knowing they won't remember it — or her. Beat: elegiac tenderness; grief for a loss that hasn't happened yet.

chapters.title: Thirteen Strokes
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, climax. At midnight she climbs the ruined tower and rings the bell through the storm while the voice pleads, threatens, and finally goes quiet with each stroke. Beat: triumphant sacrifice; the skeptic becomes the bell's believer and its jailer.

chapters.title: The Village That Forgot
chapters.summary: Maren's POV, aftermath. Morning comes clean: clocks run, songs get finished, and Maren finds an unfamiliar recorder full of tapes labeled in handwriting she almost recognizes. Beat: bittersweet resolution; salvation leaves a wound shaped like a person.

chapters.title: Keeper of the Count
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Rosalind's POV. From inside the bell's silence she watches the village live on, answering the nightly questions alone, keeping the ledger so no one else must. Final beat: haunting peace; memory, the story insists, was always the price of survival.
